Clinicians record attachment positions intraorally with six reusable titanium scan bodies, and the lab places and cures the overdenture housings without poured models, analogs, or chairside pickup.
why: Moving housing placement to the lab could remove chairside blockout and acrylic pickup steps for overdenture cases, though the excerpt does not give clinical outcome data.

headline: Smartee Presents Class II Mandibular Repositioning Approach at SIDO 2026
summary: Smartee Denti-Technology took part in the 57th SIDO International Congress in Turin, held October 8–10, discussing complex case management and digital tools in orthodontic decisions. Dr. Jingting Lu gave a clinical lecture on S8-SGTB, part of the Smartee GS system, which pairs Mandibular Repositioning Technology with clear aligners to treat severe skeletal Class II jaw discrepancies.

headline: National Poll Finds Bipartisan Backing for Dental Coverage in Medicare and Veterans Care
summary: A national poll by CareQuest Institute for Oral Health, conducted with Marketing for Change, found broad support across party lines for dental coverage, including for older or disabled adults and veterans. Nine in 10 voters backed Medicare dental coverage, with 96% of Democrats, 86% of Republicans, and 92% of Independents in favor. Traditional Medicare currently does not include dental coverage.
why: The findings suggest that expanded dental coverage in public programs has wide political support, which could shape future policy changes that affect patient access and how practices serve Medicare and veteran patients.

headline: Dentistry Unmasked episode explores when to walk away from public dental careers
summary: The latest Dentistry Unmasked episode concludes a candid conversation between Pam and Irene Iancu. It focuses on the difficulty of deciding when to step back from opportunities while building a public career in dentistry.
why: It offers a personal perspective for dentists weighing public-facing roles, though the excerpt gives no specific details or advice.

headline: Betsy Shapiro Receives ADA Distinguished Service Award at 2026 Scientific Session
summary: The American Dental Association recognized Dr. Elizabeth "Betsy" Shapiro with its Distinguished Service Award, the highest honor given by the ADA Board of Trustees, at the 2026 Scientific Session in Indianapolis. Shapiro has served the ADA for more than 15 years, currently as Chief of Governance and Strategy Management, and was interim Executive Director in 2025. Three other awards were also presented at the meeting, including the Norton M. Ross Award for Excellence in Clinical Research.
why: The recognition highlights leadership changes within the ADA, the national association that shapes policy and programs affecting practicing dentists.

headline: Implant-anchored 3D-printed titanium mesh rebuilds severe maxilla in ectodermal dysplasia case
summary: A case report describes a 24-year-old man with ectodermal dysplasia, oligodontia, and severe maxillary ridge hypoplasia who had only four permanent teeth left. Treatment combined orthodontics, restoration of remaining teeth, bilateral sinus floor elevation, and staged implant placement, with two posterior implants anchoring a custom 3D-printed titanium mesh for guided bone regeneration. Six implants were ultimately restored with fixed prostheses, and at about four years all implants were functioning with healthy peri-implant tissue and no complications.
why: It shows that patient-specific printed titanium mesh, secured by implants, can be part of a digitally planned approach to rebuilding severely deficient jaws, though this is a single case with a relatively short follow-up.

headline: Appeals court revives antitrust suit over Align's Invisalign scanner access
summary: A US federal appeals court has reinstated antitrust claims against Align Technology tied to its 2017 decision to end software interoperability between Invisalign and 3Shape intra-oral scanners. The 9th Circuit reversed a lower court's summary judgment in Align's favor, so the claims can proceed to trial.
why: The ruling could affect how Invisalign works with scanners from other manufacturers, which matters for practices choosing digital impression systems and for the competitive landscape of clear aligner workflows.

headline: NextDent 300 aims to simplify digital denture production
summary: 3D Systems has introduced the NextDent Jetted Denture Solution, an integrated approach meant to address bottlenecks in digital denture manufacturing. The excerpt notes that separate printing steps, manual assembly, post-polymerisation and lengthy finishing can erode the efficiency expected from a fully digital workflow.
why: For dentists who work with dental labs, a more streamlined denture workflow could shorten turnaround times and reduce manual steps in producing digital dentures.

headline: CareCredit Launches Pay Later Installment Option for Health and Wellness Costs
summary: CareCredit, a Synchrony solution, has launched CareCredit Pay Later, an enhanced and rebranded installment loan that gives patients a fixed payment plan with a defined payoff timeline for elective care not covered by insurance. It sits alongside CareCredit's existing credit card and is available now at nearly 20,000 locations, including select dental offices, with plans to expand across the network over time. Consumers apply once and can choose between the two products.
why: Dental practices that accept CareCredit may see more payment choices offered to patients for elective treatment, and survey data in the release suggests payment options influence both provider choice and acceptance of recommended treatment plans.

headline: Registration Opens for Spear Summit 2027 in Orlando
summary: Spear Education has opened registration for Spear Summit 2027, a four-day event running April 7–10, 2027, at the JW Marriott Orlando, Grande Lakes. The program will cover clinical topics and the business of running a dental practice, with keynotes, continuing education, an exhibit hall, and a Friday evening Signature Party. Early-bird discounts run through December 15 and can save up to $495 on registration.
why: Dentists and their teams who want continuing education with practical clinical and practice-management content can plan ahead, and early registration brings the largest discount.

headline: GuidedSMILE Gains New U.S. Patent for Guided Implant Surgery Fixation Base
summary: The USPTO issued U.S. Patent No. 12,758,365 to GuidedSMILE, covering a fixation base and guides for dental prosthesis installation, announced October 13, 2026. The patent adds 17 claims to the company's portfolio and is described as the broadest claims in the GuidedSMILE patent family to date. The company says its methodology has been used in more than 50,000 patient cases.

headline: Digital Workflow Aims to Simplify Implant-Supported Overdenture Prosthetics
summary: The article describes the ArchBridge for Overdenture digital workflow from ROE Dental Laboratory, which pairs uniquely identifiable scan bodies with digital capture of a patient's existing denture or overdenture. The workflow uses that prosthesis as a restorative template to record implant position, soft tissue, occlusion, and vertical dimension, enabling a model-free laboratory process. The authors frame it as a response to the difficulty of transferring implant position while keeping the patient's established occlusion and tooth arrangement.
why: For dentists restoring edentulous patients with implant overdentures, this offers a possible digital alternative to technique-sensitive conventional implant impressions, though the excerpt does not report outcomes or comparative accuracy data.

headline: FDA Clears First Dental-Dedicated MRI System for Soft-Tissue Diagnostics
summary: Dentsply Sirona and Siemens Healthineers have received FDA clearance in the United States for MAGNETOM Free.Max Dental Edition, described as the first MRI system dedicated to dentistry. A clinical trial reported that the system may be useful across endodontics, periodontics, TMJ, tooth extraction, and orthodontics, using non-ionizing imaging. The trial also highlighted a dental-specific field of view and an average workflow time of under 20 minutes.

headline: CareCredit Adds Pay Later Installment Loan for Elective Health Care Costs
summary: Synchrony's CareCredit has launched CareCredit Pay Later, a one-time-use installment loan with fixed monthly payments and a fixed APR for elective health and wellness costs not covered by insurance. It is available at nearly 20,000 locations, including select dental practices, and is offered alongside the traditional revolving CareCredit card through a single application. Providers also get a Provider Center payment calculator that includes the new option and can adjust loan amounts before funding.

headline: AI review analysis can surface hidden service gaps in five-star patient feedback
summary: The article argues that even positive Google reviews contain comments about wait times and other friction that teams often miss. It describes using AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini to sort and count recurring themes across a year of reviews, with three practices sharing examples at each stage of the patient visit. The piece also offers copy-and-paste AI prompts and a chart for assigning each fix to a team member.
why: Patient reviews, including praise with caveats, can be a low-cost source of insight into front-desk, paperwork, and chairside issues that practices can then assign to specific staff.

headline: Cone-beam CT study compares soft and hard tissue changes after sliding genioplasty for microgenia
summary: A retrospective cohort study from a Zhejiang University hospital used cone-beam CT three-dimensional cephalometric analysis to examine patients with microgenia who underwent advancement sliding genioplasty between January 2024 and January 2025. Patients were grouped by facial convexity angle (≤25° or >25°), and the soft-to-hard tissue movement ratio was compared between groups. The authors report a sagittal difference only at the menton and describe stable movement ratios in both sagittal and vertical chin movements.
why: The findings offer quantitative data that could help surgeons and orthodontic or surgical planners predict how the soft tissue profile will respond after chin advancement, though the excerpt does not give the full results or clinical recommendations.

headline: Single implants placed 1982-1985 show high satisfaction after nearly 39 years
summary: A cross-sectional study followed 13 patients with 18 single dental implants placed between 1982 and 1985, with a mean follow-up of 38.9 years. Patients reported high overall treatment and functional satisfaction, while esthetic ratings and professional soft-tissue scores were more variable. Incisal and cervical crown discrepancies were seen at all six assessable anterior sites, but without baseline esthetic data they cannot be attributed specifically to progressive infraposition.
why: It offers rare very-long-term evidence that single implants can keep patients satisfied, though esthetic results and soft-tissue appearance varied and the small sample limits how far the findings apply to routine practice.

headline: On-demand dosing matches scheduled analgesics for postop pain after endodontic treatment
summary: A randomized trial at a graduate endodontic clinic compared scheduled and on-demand dosing of ibuprofen and acetaminophen in emergency patients with symptomatic apical periodontitis. Of 172 enrolled patients, 126 completed diaries and returned pill counts over 3 days after treatment. Scheduled dosing led to roughly double the medication use, yet pain relief did not differ significantly between groups.
why: Dentists may consider advising patients to take ibuprofen and acetaminophen as needed rather than on a fixed schedule, which could reduce medication intake without sacrificing pain control.

headline: In vitro study compares guide printing methods and implant design in static guided surgery
summary: An in vitro study placed 80 implants in resin bone models using guides printed by either digital light processing or material extrusion. Positional deviations were smaller at healed premolar ridges than at molar extraction sites, and the two Straumann tissue-level implants differed in deviation and primary stability.
why: For guided implant placement, printing technology did not change accuracy in this lab setting, but molar extraction sites showed larger deviations and the chosen implant design affected both accuracy and stability, so extra safety margins may be warranted there until in vivo results are available.

headline: Survey of Sana'a dentists reveals gaps in TMD care under conflict conditions
summary: Researchers in Yemen surveyed dentists in Sana'a about physical therapies for temporomandibular disorder (TMD), an area where earlier studies found knowledge and use gaps. The work focused on conflict-affected healthcare settings, where little was previously known. Based on the findings, the team proposed targeted training and practical TMD management approaches suited to local constraints.
why: It points to the value of focused continuing education on physical therapy options for TMD and of treatment approaches that work within limited resources.

headline: Commentary urges explicit causal reasoning in oral health research
summary: This Journal of Periodontology commentary argues that oral health studies often present adjusted associations as causal effects despite using advanced statistics. The author proposes a four-pillar framework: defining a precise estimand, aligning study design with it, using counterfactual reasoning and directed acyclic graphs to guide adjustment, and interpreting estimates with explicit attention to causal assumptions. The framework is illustrated with a worked example on periodontal treatment and cardiovascular disease.
why: It suggests that dentists reading periodontal or systemic-health studies should look closely at whether causal claims rest on clearly stated assumptions, not just on statistical significance.

headline: Finnish study examines jaw osteonecrosis risk in breast cancer patients with bone metastases
summary: A nationwide Finnish study looked at how often medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaws (MRONJ) occurs in patients with breast cancer that has spread to bone. These patients take anti-resorptive drugs to limit bone damage, pain and fractures, and this group had not been studied before in Finland. The authors highlight the need for dental and oncology professionals to work together.
why: Dentists treating patients on anti-resorptive drugs for metastatic breast cancer should coordinate closely with the patient's oncology team to manage MRONJ risk.

headline: Rising costs squeeze DSO margins; two revenue and cost responses outlined
summary: Rising expenses are pressuring dental service organizations, according to this piece. It highlights ways DSOs can improve collections, widen patient payment options, and use compliant credit card surcharging to lower processing costs.
why: Practice owners facing higher overhead may consider collections, payment options, and compliant surcharging as ways to protect revenue and reduce card-processing fees.

headline: LumaDent Ergo Trinity Loupes Offer Three Magnifications in One Titanium Frame
summary: LumaDent's Ergo Trinity Multi-Mag TTL loupes combine 3.5x, 5.0x, and 7.0x magnification in a single titanium body, with users switching between them quickly. The loupes have a lightweight titanium build, built-in Vario WD technology for adjusting working distance with a twist, and come with a carrying case, nose pads, side shields, a cleaning cloth, and other accessories.

headline: Analysis of 150,000+ Practice Calls Reveals Gaps in Dental Front-Desk Performance
summary: An opinion piece by Dr. Nate Jeal draws on an analysis of more than 150,000 inbound calls across hundreds of dental practices. The author argues that practice owners often misjudge how well their phones and inbound patient inquiries are handled. The piece says that until recently, the calls and their outcomes were not measured at all.
why: Dentists may be missing new patients who call or submit web forms and never get a response, so measuring how inbound calls convert into booked appointments could matter for practice revenue.

headline: Directa Unica Master Kit offers matrices and wedges for anterior restorations
summary: Dr. George Freedman reviews the Polydentia Unica Master Kit, distributed by Directa USA, which includes ultra-thin stainless-steel anterior and proximal matrices in several configurations. The kit also contains myWedge anatomical interdental plastic wedges with a hollow V-shape designed to conform to interproximal anatomy.
why: Having several matrix shapes in one system lets a dentist choose a matrix suited to each tooth's morphology, which may support more controlled anterior restorations.

headline: Dental VIP Summit 2027 Set for Chicago to Link Innovators and Investors
summary: The third annual Dental VIP (Venture, Innovation & Partnering) Summit will be held Feb. 24, 2027, in Chicago, the day before the Chicago Dental Society Midwinter Meeting. The one-day event will bring together entrepreneurs, investors, clinicians, DSO leaders and industry executives, with keynotes, panels, company presentations and networking focused on AI, clinical innovation and investment.

headline: Banuba and Your Social Smile Partner on AR Smile Preview Tool
summary: Face AI company Banuba and patient engagement platform Your Social Smile (YSS) have announced a strategic partnership. The YSS Platform lets patients preview a simulation of their own smile on any device, either live in augmented reality or generated from a single photo, with no scanner or app needed.

headline: DentalXChange Appoints Scott Hampel as President
summary: DentalXChange, a revenue cycle management provider for dentistry, has named Scott Hampel as its president. He brings more than 25 years of healthcare technology leadership and will oversee the company's product, operations, and engineering teams, reporting to CEO Paul Kaiser. The company says combining those functions under one leader should speed delivery of new solutions such as Eligibility AI, Reconcile AI, PayConnect, PortalPass, and XConnect.
why: A leadership change at a dental billing and claims company may affect how quickly new tools for insurance eligibility and payment reach dental offices.

headline: Titanium Particles May Drive Persistent Inflammation Around Dental Implants
summary: A Rutgers School of Dental Medicine study, conducted in mice, found that dental implants can release tiny titanium particles when bacteria are present. These particles trigger white blood cells to stay in a hyperinflammatory state that gradually erodes bone, and closing a specific calcium channel in those cells shut down the inflammatory pathway. The article notes that antibiotics are rarely effective against peri-implantitis, and that the findings could eventually lead to medications that switch off this response.
why: It suggests a possible biological reason peri-implantitis is hard to treat with antibiotics, which may eventually lead to new drug options for keeping implants healthy long term, though current findings come from animal research.

headline: Dental sleep group asks FDA to warn consumers about OSA oral appliances
summary: The American Academy of Dental Sleep Medicine sent a letter to the FDA asking it to create a consumer webpage on oral appliances for obstructive sleep apnea. The group says these devices need a prescription or licensed-practitioner supervision to work and avoid harm. It points to an existing FDA page on clear aligners that stresses seeking care from a licensed orthodontist, and it warns that many over-the-counter OSA products lack evidence of efficacy.
why: Dentists treating sleep apnea may see patients who bought unsupervised oral appliances or over-the-counter devices, and any FDA consumer guidance could shape how patients approach these treatments.

headline: Maker of Brush Buddies, Evo and ARU Toothpastes Recalls Over 4 Million Tubes
summary: The manufacturer voluntarily recalled more than 4 million tubes of toothpaste nationwide on September 10. On October 19, the FDA classified the recall as Class II, a category for products that may cause temporary or short-lived negative health effects but not serious, lasting harm. The FDA tied the recall to failures to meet current good manufacturing practice requirements for controlling manufacturing, processing, and packaging.

headline: Quiz Covers Causes and Assessment of Tooth Wear
summary: This Decisions in Dentistry quiz tests readers on tooth wear. It covers attrition from tooth-to-tooth contact, erosion linked to bulimia nervosa, and a recommended approach to evaluating wear before choosing treatment. Most of the excerpt is sign-up and quiz navigation text.
why: The quiz reinforces a practical habit: identify the cause and pattern of tooth wear before deciding between monitoring, preventive care, or restorative treatment.

headline: Carestream launches CS 1300 intraoral camera for image capture and patient communication
summary: Carestream Dental has introduced the CS 1300 intraoral camera, aimed at producing high-quality images for patient communication and clinical documentation. It features a 280° rotating head, nine adjustable LED lights with selectable color-temperature modes, and dual autofocus with a 10–100 mm focus range. The camera works with CS Imaging version 8 and other imaging software, and connects via USB without drivers.
why: For a practice, this is a new intraoral camera option that could make chairside image capture and sharing with patients quicker, with plug-and-play setup and compatibility with existing imaging software.

headline: Coast Dental to Pay $3.8M to Settle Suit Over Unwanted Calls and Texts
summary: Coast Dental, a DSO with practices in Florida, Georgia, and Texas, agreed to pay more than $3.8 million to settle a class action alleging it violated federal and Florida telephone consumer protection laws. The suit claims the company made unsolicited calls and texts encouraging scheduling, including to people who had opted out. The company does not admit wrongdoing, and class members can choose $59 cash or a free power toothbrush (sold by the practice for $99) by October 30.
why: Practices that use phone or text marketing need documented opt-in consent and opt-out handling, since violations of these telephone laws can lead to costly class action settlements.

headline: Short case-based dental-pharmacy training improves collaboration skills in students
summary: A study evaluated a single 3-hour interprofessional session in which 118 third-year dental students and second-year pharmacy students worked through an anticoagulant case involving a patient taking apixaban before a tooth extraction. Using a retrospective pre-post survey, 19 of 20 self-rated collaboration competencies improved significantly, with small-to-moderate effect sizes. Students also described clearer understanding of each profession's role and greater confidence communicating across disciplines, though scheduling and instruction problems reduced engagement for some.
why: It suggests that brief, case-focused training with pharmacists may help dentists coordinate safely on medically complex patients on high-risk medications, and that clear logistics matter for making such training work.

headline: Systematic review compares diagnostic tests for peripheral trigeminal nerve injuries
summary: A systematic review of 10 studies (520 participants, 514 nerves) assessed how accurately methods detect peripheral trigeminal nerve injuries in the maxillary and mandibular regions after oral and maxillofacial procedures. Clinical neurosensory testing performed well for lingual nerve injuries but worse for inferior alveolar nerve injuries, while the tongue somatosensory evoked magnetic field laterality index had the highest single-test accuracy for lingual nerve injury. The authors concluded that a multimodal diagnostic approach is supported.
why: Dentists managing nerve sensation problems after extractions, implant or surgical procedures may find that no single test is reliable, so combining clinical testing with other methods may give a more accurate picture of injury.

headline: Salivary vesicles shift after non-surgical periodontal therapy in periodontitis patients
summary: In a longitudinal study of 25 patients with stage III/IV periodontitis, researchers tracked host and microbial extracellular vesicles in saliva at baseline and at 3 and 6 months after non-surgical periodontal therapy. Periodontal parameters improved at both follow-up points, with rises in certain host-vesicle cytokines (IL-4, IL-12, IL-9) and declines in bacterial vesicles and matching bacterial taxa in saliva and plaque. At 6 months, one fungal vesicle source fell while a Candida parapsilosis source rose.

headline: Extraoral scan body design affects accuracy of digital facial-intraoral patient models
summary: This observational clinical study compared how extraoral scan body designs affect the trueness and precision of virtual patient models built from facial scans merged with intraoral scans. Ten participants were scanned with one professional facial scanner (MetiSmile) and three smartphone-based scanners (EM3D, Heges, Qlone), using a tooth-based method or five different scan body designs. Tooth-based integration gave better trueness than scan body workflows for the professional scanner and EM3D, the scan body design significantly affected trueness across all scanners, and MetiSmile had the best trueness overall.
why: Dentists using facial scanning for virtual dentofacial analysis should know that the integration method and scan body design can change the accuracy of the resulting patient model, so these choices matter when planning digital workflows.

headline: Facial hair affects accuracy of virtual patient models from facial scanners
summary: A clinical study of 10 male participants compared how clean-shaven, stubble, and bearded faces affected the accuracy of virtual patient representations built from three professional facial scanners and one smartphone-based scanner. Facial hair style significantly affected accuracy only for smiling scans, and the effect depended on which scanner was used. For one professional scanner, a dedicated beard mode improved accuracy for full beards but worsened it for stubble.
why: Dentists using facial scans merged with intraoral scans for digital planning should be aware that facial hair and scanner choice can change accuracy, especially for smile captures.

headline: Digital workflow for bimaxillary complete-arch implant rehabilitation with immediate loading
summary: A clinical report describes a digitally assisted protocol for full-arch implant treatment in both jaws of a 70-year-old edentulous man. The team used stackable surgical guides, a double-scan virtual planning method, and immediate loading of all but one implant. Six months later, segmented zirconia and lithium disilicate restorations were delivered, and the authors reported favorable functional, esthetic, and biologic outcomes.
why: It shows a single-patient example of how a double-scan digital plan with stackable guides can guide bimaxillary immediate-load implant cases, though one case report offers limited evidence for routine adoption.

headline: Custom trays showed better trueness than stock trays in complete arch implant impressions
summary: An in vitro study compared stock and custom impression trays, with and without heavy-body PVS subsplint reinforcement, for maxillary complete arch implant impressions. The primary analysis found custom trays gave more accurate casts than stock trays, while subsplint reinforcement did not significantly improve trueness and no interaction was found. The tray effect was not consistent across all statistical methods, so the authors urge caution in interpreting it.

headline: Postprint cleaning time and glaze choice shape 3D-printed resin strength and color
summary: An in vitro study tested four 3D-printed A2 resin composites under different cleaning durations and surface glazing agents, measuring flexural strength, surface roughness, and color stability. Material type, cleaning duration, and glazing all significantly affected the outcomes, and glazing reduced roughness, improved color stability, and raised flexural strength, with Palaseal performing best overall. Longer cleaning generally increased strength and roughness on unglazed specimens, and the ideal cleaning time varied by material.
why: Postprocessing steps such as cleaning time and glazing appear to meaningfully change how printed resin restorations perform, so protocols for these steps matter for the durability and appearance of chairside or lab-printed restorations.

headline: In vitro study compares intraoral, reverse, and photogrammetry recordings for complete-arch implants
summary: Researchers compared three digital recording methods for a complete maxillary implant arch with six multi-unit abutments: intraoral scanning, reverse scanning, and stereophotogrammetry, with 15 recordings per method. Reverse scanning had the best linear trueness (39.1 µm), followed by intraoral scanning (69.7 µm) and stereophotogrammetry (102.8 µm). Reverse scanning had the worst angular trueness, and its angular error was above the clinically acceptable threshold, while precision did not differ significantly among the methods.
why: For complete-arch implant cases, reverse scanning may offer good linear accuracy but its angular error suggests limited clinical use for now, so intraoral scanning may remain the more reliable choice for angular fit.

headline: Review weighs therapeutic-ion bioactive glasses for vital pulp therapy
summary: This critical narrative review in Dental Materials examines whether bioactive glasses doped with therapeutic ions can control microbes and modulate immune responses in the pulp while keeping pulp cells viable and supporting reparative dentin. It compares silicate, phosphate, and borate-based glasses and assesses Ag, Zn, Sr, Li, Ce, Ga, and emerging Cu- and Co-containing systems. The authors conclude that current evidence is mostly preclinical, often lacks matched ion release, pH, and biological measurements, and that no dopant or safe concentration can be chosen on ion identity alone.
why: Dentists considering bioactive materials for vital pulp therapy should treat ion-doped glasses as still experimental, since the review finds no established safe concentration and little direct clinical outcome data.

headline: Glass coating method improves bonding to ultra-translucent zirconia in lab study
summary: Researchers developed an experimental SiO₂-Li₂O-Al₂O₃ glass-ceramic coating for ultra-translucent zirconia (5Y-PSZ) and compared it with a commercial glass-ceramic coating, Biomic LiSi Connect. Across 110 specimens, both coatings produced a glass-rich surface and enhanced optical properties, and longer 60-second hydrofluoric acid etching increased shear bond strength. The experimental coating also showed stable bonding after 5000 thermal cycles, with mostly mixed or cohesive failures.
why: This suggests a possible way to improve adhesion of translucent zirconia restorations without compromising their aesthetic properties, though it remains a lab study with no clinical outcomes reported.

headline: Brazilian dentists often over-treat direct resin restorations versus FDI criteria
summary: In a diagnostic accuracy study, 394 Brazilian dentists chose management options for posterior resin-based restorations in clinical scenarios and their choices were compared with FDI-based reference decisions. Overall accuracy was 44.8%, with fair agreement (kappa 0.27), and over-treatment occurred about seven times more often than under-treatment. Replacement was chosen far more often than the reference indicated, and scenario type explained more of the variation than the individual dentist did; education and time since graduation showed only limited associations with accuracy.
why: It suggests many dentists may replace restorations that could be reviewed, refurbished, or repaired, which would remove more sound tooth structure, so conservative options deserve emphasis in training and practice.

headline: Smaller filler particles improve initial strength of 3D-printed resins but add print time
summary: Researchers compared two highly filled experimental 3D-printed dental resins containing silanized barium glass of 1.5 µm or 0.7 µm particle size, printed by digital light processing. Before thermocycling, the finer 0.7 µm formulation had higher flexural strength and elastic modulus and lower surface roughness, but these gains were not kept after thermocycling. The finer formulation also took far longer to fabricate (about 122 minutes versus 48 minutes), and no advantage was found for microhardness or shear bond strength.
why: Finer filler may strengthen printed resins initially, but the benefit faded after aging and printing took much longer, so particle size is a trade-off to weigh when choosing printable materials.

source: Oral Surg Oral Med Oral Pathol Oral Radiol
headline: Areca (betel) nut use rising in US and what it means for dental practice
summary: A narrative review examines areca nut, also called betel nut, which is abused as a psychostimulant and is the fourth most commonly abused psychoactive substance globally. Its use is strongly linked to potentially malignant oral disorders such as leukoplakia and oral submucous fibrosis, as well as oral cancers, staining, dentin hypersensitivity, periodontal disease, and betel chewer's mucosa. The authors note growing use in the United States due to immigration from regions where the habit is common, and they cover US regulations, US-based user studies, and knowledge gaps.
why: US dentists may see more patients who chew areca nut without recognizing the habit, so learning to identify users and manage its oral effects, including precancerous lesions, is increasingly important.

headline: Triangular osteotomy limits chin widening versus horizontal cut in sliding genioplasty
summary: A retrospective cohort study from 2020 to 2025 compared modified triangular and conventional horizontal osteotomy designs in 32 adults with chin retrognathia who had 8-mm advancement genioplasty using 3D-printed templates. At 3 months, the triangular group showed smaller increases in labiomental sulcus depth and chin width than the horizontal group, and it reached the predefined bony mentolabial angle target more often. The soft tissue mentolabial angle change did not differ significantly between groups.
why: For surgeons planning advancement genioplasty, osteotomy design appears to affect postoperative chin width and angle outcomes, so the choice of cut may matter for predictable contour results.

headline: Historical profile of dentist J. E. H. Duckworth and his opposition to a dental NHS
summary: This British Dental Journal historical paper profiles J. E. H. Duckworth, a London dental practitioner who served in the First World War and later set up practice in North London. During the Second World War he was active in the Group Movement, which grew out of local committees supporting dentists on military service and helped unite the profession's representative bodies. The paper draws on his monthly London Dental Circular to examine the arguments he and the Movement made against a national dental service.
why: It offers historical context on how the profession's internal politics shaped debates over the NHS's introduction, which informs understanding of current dental policy debates.

headline: Lip fillers can change orthodontic assessment and treatment planning, review finds
summary: A literature review in the British Dental Journal looks at how lip filler augmentation, which alters lip contour and volume, affects orthodontic practice. It examines how different filler materials and injection techniques influence key assessment parameters. The authors also offer practical recommendations for spotting patients who have had lip augmentation, timing assessments relative to filler placement, and communicating across disciplines.
why: Dentists doing orthodontic assessments may encounter patients with recent lip fillers that change smile aesthetics and facial profile, so recognizing them and coordinating timing and communication with other providers can shape treatment planning.

headline: Sublingual gland carcinoma initially mistaken for salivary stone underscores need for re-assessment
summary: A case report describes a 31-year-old woman referred for a hard floor-of-mouth swelling thought to be a salivary calculus, where plain radiography showed no radiopacity and ultrasound appeared to support the calculus diagnosis. After three months, with loosening lower anterior teeth and growing swelling, imaging revealed a large defect in the anterior mandible, and the lesion was diagnosed as a poorly differentiated salivary carcinoma of the sublingual gland with lung, brain and spine metastases. The patient died ten months after diagnosis.
why: Persistent or progressing swelling that does not match an apparently benign finding, such as a suspected sialolith, should prompt timely re-examination and imaging, since rare malignant salivary tumours can present in this way.

headline: Review identifies communication phrases for trauma-informed care in oral health
summary: A concise review in the British Dental Journal searched databases and grey literature for communication phrases that support trauma-informed care in oral health. Eight papers out of 27 full-text articles contained such phrases, which were grouped by clinical situation, such as before treatment, screening for trauma, and motivational interviewing. The authors conclude the phrases may be a practical tool but need further research to confirm they work.
why: Dentists who want to care for patients with trauma histories may find a set of ready-to-use phrases helpful, though the evidence for their effectiveness is still limited.

headline: Oral health proposed as a lever for UK health system transformation
summary: A Br Dent J paper argues that oral health is an underused tool for reforming the UK health system, since oral conditions are among the most common noncommunicable diseases yet are still dominated by costly intervention-based care. It calls for a shift toward prevention, integration into primary care, and equity, while noting Scotland's Childsmile Programme as evidence of cost-effective prevention. The authors also stress addressing social determinants such as education, housing, nutrition and income, along with workforce reform, technology, and political and civil society support.
why: It suggests that dental teams may increasingly be expected to work within primary care and community prevention models, and that policy direction in the UK may shift toward prevention-focused funding and workforce changes.

headline: Microgrooved BMP-2 membranes show early bone gain and ridge preservation in animal models
summary: Researchers tested a barrier membrane with V-shaped microgrooves, reinforced with electrospun PCL fibers and loaded with rhBMP-2, for alveolar ridge preservation after extraction. In rat calvarial defects, the grooved membranes sped early healing and, with rhBMP-2, nearly closed the defect within 2 weeks. In beagles, treated extraction sockets kept ridge width, height and the buccal bone plate at 3 months compared with natural healing.
why: If these findings hold in humans, a membrane that actively guides early bone sealing could offer a way to limit post-extraction ridge loss, which matters for implant planning, though this work is limited to animal studies so far.

headline: Prenatal phthalate and BPA exposure linked to hypomineralized second primary molars in a Dutch cohort
summary: Researchers using the Generation R birth cohort in the Netherlands measured maternal urinary BPA and 11 phthalate metabolites each trimester and assessed hypomineralized second primary molars (HSPM) at age 6 in 1,160 mother-child pairs. Higher prenatal monobenzyl phthalate was associated with lower odds of HSPM overall, while associations for BPA and phthalates differed by sex, with lower odds in girls and higher odds in boys. Overall mixture associations were not statistically significant.
why: The findings are preliminary and mixed, with sex-specific and non-significant results, so they do not yet change how HSPM is diagnosed or managed, but they add human evidence that early-life endocrine-disrupting chemical exposure may play a role in enamel development.

headline: Oral health gaps among older adults in England have persisted and partly widened
summary: Using data from the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing, researchers tracked oral health by education, occupation, household income and wealth among older adults from 2006-2007 to 2018-2019. Tooth loss declined over the period, while reports of oral impacts on daily life and fair or poor self-rated oral health rose. Socioeconomic gradients were present for all outcomes, with relative gaps staying largely stable and absolute gaps narrowing for tooth loss but widening for self-rated oral health and oral impacts.
why: Dentists treating older patients should expect socioeconomic disparities in oral health to persist, supporting the case for upstream prevention and attention to patients' everyday oral impacts, not just tooth loss.

headline: Multi-omics study maps nonlinear progression and molecular subtypes in TMJ disease
summary: Researchers profiled synovial fluid proteins and metabolites from TMJ patients across five imaging-defined stages, from normal disc to advanced degeneration with perforation. Symptoms did not differ significantly between stages, and molecular profiles did not separate by stage, though severity scores rose from stage 1 to stage 4 and dropped at stage 5. The team reported three exploratory molecular subtypes that complement anatomical staging, and flagged PLTP and FSTL1 as candidate markers linked to severity.
why: It suggests that imaging stage alone may not explain why patients with similar scans have different clinical courses, pointing toward future molecular stratification, though these findings are exploratory and not yet applicable to clinical decisions.

headline: pH-responsive cobalt sulfide nanozyme shows promise against cariogenic biofilms in rats
summary: Researchers developed a positively charged, polyethyleneimine-coated cobalt sulfide nanozyme that becomes catalytically active mainly under acidic conditions. In lab tests it killed Streptococcus mutans, disrupted mature biofilms, and in a rat caries model reduced smooth and sulcal surface caries while keeping overall oral microbial diversity intact.

headline: CaneStat recombinant protein shapes pellicle and reduces early enamel erosion in vivo
summary: Researchers tested CaneStat, a recombinant hybrid protein, on hydroxyapatite sensors and in a randomized, triple-blind crossover trial with 18 healthy volunteers. Compared with a deionized water negative control, CaneStat at 0.025 mg/mL and the Elmex positive control both showed higher surface reflection intensity values after pellicle formation times of 3 minutes and 2 hours before an erosive challenge. The authors concluded that CaneStat forms a pellicle with distinct physicochemical properties and is associated with greater early erosion resistance.
why: This early-stage study suggests a protein-based agent could offer a new approach to preventing dental erosion, though it remains a short-term, single-concentration result that needs further clinical validation before changing patient recommendations.

headline: State Cigarette Taxes Cut Smoking but Show No Clear Link to Tooth Loss
summary: Using 15 cycles of US Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System data from 1995 to 2012 (N = 3,840,519), researchers examined how state cigarette taxes, retail prices, and indoor smoking bans related to smoking and tooth loss. Higher cigarette taxes and prices were linked to less current smoking and more quitting, but no robust effect on tooth loss was found. Indoor smoking bans were not associated with lower smoking or less tooth loss.

headline: Screen time linked to worse oral health quality of life in 12-year-olds
summary: A longitudinal study of 610 twelve-year-old students in public schools in Manaus, Brazil, examined how screen time relates to oral health and oral health-related quality of life. Screen time was not directly tied to clinical oral conditions, but it was associated with a greater impact on quality of life and less frequent toothbrushing. Higher sugar intake and poorer clinical oral condition were also linked to a greater quality-of-life impact, and socioeconomic status shaped several of these pathways.
why: For pediatric and general practice, this suggests that screen habits, family context, and socioeconomic background may matter alongside diet and brushing when assessing young patients' oral health and counseling their families.

headline: Two mandibular setback methods for class III high-angle bite compared in prospective study
summary: This prospective study compared two ways of performing counterclockwise mandibular setback within surgery-first bimaxillary surgery for skeletal class III high-angle malocclusion. Fifty-six adults were divided by whether the mandibular distal segment was shortened (25 patients) or lengthened (31 patients), and CBCT measurements were tracked from before treatment to 1 week after surgery and to post-treatment. Both groups showed sagittal relapse of the mandible, but post-treatment outcomes were largely similar, with the shortening group showing smaller jaw projection and upper incisor angle.
why: For surgeons planning orthognathic correction of high-angle class III cases, the findings suggest both posterior-shortening and posterior-lengthening setback can be effective when matched to each patient's skeletal and occlusal features, though some post-surgical relapse should be expected.

headline: Augmented reality implant guidance more angularly accurate than templates in bone models
summary: An in-vitro study compared implants placed with augmented reality (HoloLens 2) against those placed with conventional drilling templates in 20 maxillary bone models, with four implants per model. AR placement showed significantly lower angular deviation (mean 1.48° vs 2.65°), while depth deviation did not differ between the two methods (about -0.07 mm vs -0.08 mm). The authors describe both methods as highly precise, with AR being more accurate for the angular outcome.
why: For dentists considering guided implant surgery, this lab study suggests AR guidance may improve angular placement accuracy over templates, though it was performed on models rather than patients and does not establish clinical benefit.

headline: Bibliometric review charts shift toward digital workflows in jaw fracture research
summary: A bibliometric analysis of 842 English-language original articles on mandibular and maxillary fractures, indexed in Scopus from 2005 to 2026, found publication output accelerating after 2020. India, China, and the United States ranked highest by corresponding author country, and 11.4% of papers had international coauthorship. Keywords such as three-dimensional printing, computed tomography, and navigation rose quickly after 2020, with 3D printing showing the highest citation impact among these digital terms.
why: It indicates that research attention is moving toward digitally assisted fracture management, though the authors state this reflects research focus rather than proven clinical superiority of the newer technologies.

headline: BRAF/MEK Inhibitors Used Before Surgery for a Pediatric Ameloblastoma Case
summary: A case report describes a 13-year-old boy with mural unicystic ameloblastoma carrying a BRAF mutation. The patient was treated with decompression and stenting, then dabrafenib plus trametinib to shrink the tumor, followed by definitive enucleation, with 30 months of follow-up. The authors note that enucleation alone of this subtype often leads to recurrence, and that targeted drug therapy against BRAF V600E has shown promising results.
why: It suggests that molecular targeted drugs may one day reduce surgical morbidity for young patients with aggressive jaw tumors, though this is a single case and not yet standard care.

headline: Bidimensional T-loop springs yield higher forces in finite element model
summary: A 3-dimensional finite element study compared bidimensional T-loop closing springs with conventional T-loops at 6, 8, and 10 mm interbracket distances and 2 mm and 4 mm activations. The bidimensional designs, which include a 90° torsion bend at the loop midportion, produced consistently higher horizontal forces and moments. The authors describe these as theoretical predictions that still need clinical and experimental validation.
why: If validated, the bidimensional T-loop could offer more anterior torque control during extraction space closure, but for now it remains a modeling result without clinical evidence.

headline: Pain intensity, not pain extent, tracks disability in temporomandibular disorder patients
summary: A cross-sectional study of 114 Iranian patients with temporomandibular disorders compared pain drawings with pain intensity scores and clinical and psychosocial measures. Pain intensity (Characteristic Pain Intensity from the Graded Chronic Pain Scale) was significantly linked to pain-related disability, while pain extent from head and neck drawings showed no significant association with disability, jaw function, or psychosocial variables. Neither measure differed by sex or pain laterality.
why: When assessing TMD patients, pain intensity appears to be a more useful indicator of functional impact than the spread of pain shown on pain drawings, which should be treated as a supplementary descriptive tool.

headline: 3D-printed bruxism splints perform comparably to milled splints over three months
summary: An exploratory cohort study of 17 patients with probable bruxism compared milled and 3D-printed stabilization splints, each worn for three months in randomized order. No significant differences were found between the two types in quality of life, antagonist wear, splint wear or retention. The 3D-printed splints needed less adjustment at insertion and were preferred by most participants for comfort, though the authors attribute these two points to the splint design rather than the manufacturing method.
why: Short-term results suggest 3D-printed stabilization splints are a clinically feasible alternative to milled splints, but the authors say long-term performance still needs study.

headline: Dental office appearance shapes lay perceptions, with intermediate and luxury designs rated similarly
summary: A cross-sectional study of 120 adults aged 18 to 65 used AI-generated images of simple, intermediate, and luxurious dental offices to see how each looked to laypeople. Participants rated the simple office substantially less favorably across trust, quality of care, hygiene and safety, equipment, technology, and recommendation, while intermediate and luxurious offices did not differ significantly from each other after statistical adjustment.
why: Clinic design appears to influence how patients judge a dentist's credibility, and a well-organized, mid-level setup may be perceived about as well as a high-end one, which matters for investment decisions in office design.

headline: BOPPPS framework with case and problem-based learning improves oral pathology teaching
summary: A randomized teaching reform study assigned 206 undergraduate oral medicine students either to a six-phase BOPPPS instructional framework that embedded case- and problem-based learning or to a traditional lecture-based control group. The reform group scored significantly higher on the oral pathology theory exam and performed better on diagnostic image recognition, especially items testing clinical reasoning. Students rated their learning experience highly, with a mean self-assessed outcome score of 4.5 out of 5.
why: It offers dental educators a structured, participatory teaching model that may strengthen students' diagnostic reasoning in oral pathology, a core skill for future clinicians.

headline: Survey finds dentists rate TMD training poorly and often recognize their knowledge limits
summary: A survey of 296 dentists examined their education, knowledge, attitudes and behavior related to temporomandibular disorders (TMD), which the excerpt says affect 5%-12% of US adults. Only a small share were satisfied with their classroom or clinic TMD training, and while most recognized their limits in managing TMD, just over a third felt confident in their knowledge. Dentists who knew more people with TMD, or who had TMD themselves (43%), reported more positive attitudes, greater comfort treating it, and more care for patients with TMD.
why: It suggests dental and continuing education on TMD may need more hands-on training, and that dentists' personal experience with TMD is linked to how they approach these patients.

headline: Education model proposed to build TMD care capacity in low- and middle-income countries
summary: A Journal of Dental Education article describes temporomandibular disorders as a range of problems involving the jaw joint, chewing muscles and nearby structures. It notes that access to TMD care is markedly unequal across the treatment continuum. The authors propose an education-centered model that trains both clinical and technical skills so low- and middle-income countries can eventually sustain TMD care locally.
why: It highlights a gap in access to TMD training and care worldwide, and suggests that structured education, rather than outside treatment alone, is the route to lasting local capability.

headline: Study identifies drivers of patient dropout before orthodontic treatment in education clinic
summary: This cross-sectional study reviewed records from 2022 to 2024 at an advanced orthodontic education clinic to find why patients stopped care before treatment despite being advised to proceed. Overall attrition fell from 51.2% after the screening appointment to 24.1% after the records appointment. Among Medicaid patients, dropout rose as the estimated likelihood of obtaining Medicaid coverage declined, and older age and orthognathic surgery plans were linked to higher attrition at different stages.
why: Dentists running orthodontic programs may see pretreatment dropout concentrated among older patients, surgical cases, and those with uncertain Medicaid coverage, so early coverage checks and clear counseling on surgical plans may help retain patients.

headline: Caries, periodontitis and tooth loss linked to higher primary liver cancer risk in Swedish cohort
summary: A large Swedish registry study of about 5.9 million adults followed for a mean of 6.36 years found that caries, periodontitis and tooth loss were each associated with a higher risk of primary liver cancer. Risk rose as the number of remaining teeth fell, and periodontitis was linked mainly to hepatocellular carcinoma while caries was linked mainly to other liver cancer subtypes. Sibling-comparison and sensitivity analyses gave generally consistent results.
why: These findings add to evidence that oral health may be connected to systemic cancer risk, which reinforces the value of caries and periodontal management and tooth retention, though the study shows association rather than cause.

headline: Polyurethane resin cement with antibacterial DMAHDM shows promise in lab tests
summary: Researchers developed a polyurethane resin cement for bonding indirect restorations that includes DMAHDM, an antibacterial monomer, aimed at reducing secondary caries. At 3% DMAHDM, the cement kept mechanical properties close to a commercial comparator and showed strong antibacterial activity against several oral bacteria, with 4-5 log10 reductions in bacterial viability. Higher concentrations (4-5%) reduced flexural strength and increased polymerization shrinkage, and the authors say clinical studies are still needed.
why: This is early laboratory and animal work, so it does not yet change how dentists bond restorations, but it signals a possible future cement option aimed at lowering secondary caries risk.

headline: Sleep and awake bruxism linked to mental health conditions in Brazilian cohort
summary: A cross-sectional analysis of the 1982 Pelotas Birth Cohort in Southern Brazil examined self-reported sleep and awake bruxism at age 40 alongside common mental disorders and specific psychiatric diagnoses. Both forms of bruxism were more common among women and people with alcohol dependence, and depression was associated with higher prevalence of each. Participants with probable common mental disorders at both age 30 and age 40 had the strongest associations with bruxism.
why: For dentists, this suggests patients reporting grinding or clenching may also have mental health concerns, so asking about mood and alcohol use could be a useful part of assessing bruxism.

headline: AI in dentistry brings practice gains and new risks, says Part 6 of series
summary: This installment of a Dental Tribune series says artificial intelligence and augmented intelligence are quickly spreading into dental work, touching imaging, documentation, treatment planning, patient communication and office administration. It notes the technology can improve care and efficiency but needs careful leadership and cannot replace the dentist's clinical judgment. As software reaches more patient data and produces content or takes actions on its own, the article says practices must weigh privacy, oversight, accuracy and verification.
why: Dentists adopting AI tools should plan for patient privacy, human oversight and verification of outputs, since the clinician remains responsible for diagnosis and treatment.

headline: Patient satisfaction with implants over 5 years tied to pre-treatment information and fewer complications
summary: This cross-sectional study surveyed 260 patients whose dental implants had been placed more than five years earlier, asking about functional, aesthetic, psychosocial and economic satisfaction. Overall satisfaction was high, with 93.1% of respondents satisfied or very satisfied. The strongest independent factors linked to satisfaction were the amount of information patients received before treatment and the absence of self-reported peri-implant inflammation, while demographics, cost and extent of rehabilitation were not associated with satisfaction.
why: Patients who felt well informed before treatment and who reported no peri-implant problems were more satisfied long term, suggesting that thorough pre-treatment counseling and ongoing maintenance may matter as much as demographics for outcomes; because the design is cross-sectional and self-reported, the link is associational rather than causal.

headline: Chairside fully guided implants improve accuracy; bone-level gains not significant after adjustment
summary: A 1-year follow-up of a randomized trial compared chairside fully guided flapless implant placement with conventional partially guided open-flap placement in patients who also had transcrestal sinus augmentation. Of 56 randomized patients, 21 fully guided and 22 partially guided patients completed follow-up. The fully guided group had better placement accuracy, while between-group differences in marginal bone level change were not statistically significant after adjustment for multiple comparisons.

headline: Wnt agonist peptide L803-mts shows reparative dentinogenesis in vitro and in rats
summary: Researchers tested L803-mts, a GSK-3β inhibitory peptide, on dental pulp stem cells and macrophages under inflammatory conditions, and in a rat pulp injury model. The peptide was studied for odontogenic differentiation, macrophage polarization, and dentine repair, with MTA as a comparison. The excerpt indicates the peptide acted through Wnt signalling activation and immunomodulation to promote reparative dentinogenesis.
why: This is preclinical work suggesting a biologically active agent could support vital pulp therapy beyond simply forming a dentine barrier, but it remains animal and lab evidence without clinical use yet.

headline: Proposed "2+4+1" dental education model aims to cut costs and boost rural workforce
summary: A Journal of Dental Education narrative review proposes a post-high school "2+4+1" model to address dental workforce shortages, rising education costs, and the relevance of licensure exams. The model combines two years of integrated pre-professional undergraduate study, a traditional four-year DDS/DMD program, and a seventh year spent in supervised rural or underserved service or in a CODA-accredited residency. Graduates would receive a limited practice-under-supervision permit, with full licensure tied to completing the seventh year or residency.
why: If adopted, the model could lower educational debt and expand access in underserved areas, but it is a proposal only and would change how new dentists enter practice.

headline: Graft resorption behavior may shape long-term implant success after ridge preservation
summary: The article argues that bone grafts placed after extraction should be gradually replaced by vital bone, since that resorption determines bone-to-implant contact later. It contrasts this with dense, heat-treated materials such as ceramic hydroxyapatite and heat-treated bovine xenografts, which the body struggles to resorb and which may become encapsulated by connective tissue. The piece also introduces OsteoGen, a non-sintered graft described as working through bioactive ion exchange with phosphate, calcium, and hydroxyl ions.
why: When choosing a graft for ridge preservation, the material's resorption behavior may affect how well implants integrate and hold up under load later, so graft selection deserves attention beyond immediate socket filling.

headline: Dr. Jacob Dent discusses special needs dentistry and desensitization techniques
summary: In an interview with Dentistry Today's editor-in-chief, special needs dentist Jacob R. Dent, DDS, discusses dental care for patients with intellectual and developmental disabilities and dental anxiety. He covers how sensory sensitivities affect visits, the Dental Desensitization Systems kit, and home oral hygiene strategies for caregivers. The conversation also touches on minimally invasive options such as silver diamine fluoride and the SMART restorative technique, and on the restorative cement Directa's Ceramir Crown & Bridge in his workflow. The interview is sponsored by Directa USA.
why: It offers practical ideas for adapting the environment and treatment approach for anxious or sensory-sensitive patients, though the excerpt is a sponsored interview and gives few specific clinical details.

headline: Universal Composites Reshape Placement Habits for Anterior and Posterior Restorations
summary: Two clinicians describe how universal nanohybrid composites have moved beyond the amalgam-centered posterior approach taught in earlier dental training. They focus on GrandioSO 4U (VOCO) as a single material for both anterior and posterior indications. The article also argues that clinicians should reassess the incremental layering standard, with implications for outcomes, workflow, and practice profitability.
why: Dentists may need to reconsider long-standing placement habits, such as reliance on amalgam for larger posterior cases and strict incremental layering, as universal composites take on a broader role.

headline: AI Visual Overlays and Plaque Disclosure Aid Patient Coaching in Dentistry
summary: A dentist writing in Dentistry Today argues that patients change behavior more readily when they can see findings such as plaque, bone loss, and demineralization. AI platforms like Overjet convert radiographic findings into color-coded overlays to help explain them, building on older tools like plaque disclosure that show retained biofilm. The piece notes that these in-office moments are important, but that daily oral health decisions happen at home.
why: Visual tools such as AI-enhanced radiographs and plaque disclosure may help dentists explain findings and motivate patients to change home care habits, though the excerpt does not report outcome data.

headline: Align Technology Commits $1 Million to AAO Foundation Over Five Years
summary: Align Technology has announced a new $1 million, five-year commitment to the American Association of Orthodontists Foundation, following a $1 million pledge it made in 2021. The funding supports the Foundation's Full-time Faculty Fellowship Campaign, which aims to endow orthodontic faculty fellowships at dental schools in the United States and Canada. Since 1994, the Foundation's Awards Program has provided $17.7 million in funding for 297 fellowships and 404 research grants.
why: The pledge reflects continued corporate investment in orthodontic education and faculty development, which supports the training pipeline for future orthodontists.

headline: SprintRay unveils wireless intra-oral scanner and compact chairside printing system
summary: SprintRay, a German-based dental technology company, showed an expanded digital dentistry platform at 3DNext 2026 in Miami Beach. The lineup includes the Foundation wireless intra-oral scanner, its ScanOS scanning software, and the Nano Series compact chairside production system. The company also announced a new restorative resin developed with GC Corp.

headline: USOSM Surgeon Volunteers at Colorado Mission of Mercy Free Clinic in Cripple Creek
summary: Oral and maxillofacial surgeon Michael Daetwyler, DDS, of Fort Collins Oral & Maxillofacial Surgery, volunteered at the 19th annual Colorado Mission of Mercy free clinic in Cripple Creek, Colorado. He spent the day mainly extracting severely decayed teeth, with the oral surgery department set up in a large tent outside the local high school. According to COMOM, more than 140 dentist volunteers treated more than 1,000 patients.
why: It shows how volunteer dental clinics can deliver large amounts of care in a single day, and how oral surgeons and general dentists can contribute to community access-to-care efforts.

headline: SoftSmile Unveils Vision Forecast AI Module for Orthodontic Case Planning
summary: SoftSmile has launched Vision Forecast, an AI-powered decision-support module within its VISION Portal that helps orthodontists assess case complexity, compare treatment options, and estimate treatment duration. It generates case summaries with approximate aligner requirements, clinical details, and common treatment strategies, such as comparing treatment with and without extractions. The company says the module will also show doctors similar past cases and how they were handled, and that it can be used to walk patients through the initial assessment.
why: Orthodontists could use AI-generated case summaries and timeline comparisons during early consultations to explain likely treatment commitment to patients before they decide on a plan.

headline: Align Technology Commits $1 Million to AAO Foundation Faculty Fellowships
summary: Align Technology has pledged $1 million over five years to the AAO Foundation, adding to a $1 million pledge it made in 2021. The funding supports the foundation's three-year Full-time Faculty Fellowship Campaign, launched in 2024, which aims to endow three two-year fellowships for orthodontic faculty at US and Canadian dental schools.
why: The campaign targets the supply of full-time orthodontic educators and researchers who train future orthodontists, which matters for dentists considering orthodontic training or referral pipelines.

headline: Topical Teriparatide on Implant Surfaces Aids Bone Integration in Rats Under Osteoporosis-Like Conditions
summary: Researchers coated titanium implants with teriparatide using a layer-by-layer topical delivery method and placed them in the maxillae of ovariectomized rats fed a cafeteria diet, some also given risedronate. After 28 days, the coated implants showed higher removal torque across all groups, with the largest gain in the rats receiving risedronate, and greater peri-implant bone volume in the two ovariectomized groups. Gene markers for bone formation and blood vessel growth were also upregulated.

headline: CBCT study links mandibular symphysis shape to vertical skeletal pattern and incisor tilt
summary: A retrospective CBCT study of 108 adults examined how mandibular symphysis morphology relates to lower incisor inclination across sagittal and vertical skeletal patterns. Vertical patterns showed significant variation in symphyseal measurements, while sagittal groups did not. Patients with hyperdivergence had larger symphyseal ratios and narrower apical widths.
why: For orthodontic planning, the study suggests that vertical facial pattern and incisor position should be assessed individually with CBCT, since symphysis shape appears to track vertical rather than sagittal skeletal differences.

headline: New eating difficulty signals broader frailty, not an oral cause of cognitive decline
summary: A study pooling four long-running ageing cohorts from China, England, the United States and Europe tested whether newly reported eating difficulty or dental problems came before sudden cognitive decline. Across 219,047 participants, eating difficulty was linked to higher dementia-indicator risk over six years, while tooth loss or poor dental health showed little adjusted association. Eating difficulty appeared to mark wider functional vulnerability, and there was no sign of an abrupt drop in cognition following its onset.
why: Eating difficulty reported in a dental or primary-care visit may prompt a broader functional and cognitive check, but the authors caution it should not be used alone as an oral-specific dementia screening test.

headline: Fit of zirconia three-unit bridges depends on how it is measured
summary: An in vitro study compared digital, semi-digital, and conventional silicone replica methods for assessing the fit of three-unit zirconia fixed dental prostheses made by additive or subtractive manufacturing. Gap values differed by material and by assessment method, and the 3D replica method gave the highest values within each material. Group mean gaps exceeded the designed cement space, and the alternative methods did not reliably substitute for the conventional one.

headline: Coded healing abutment transfer accuracy varies by scanner and implant site
summary: An in vitro study compared single-implant digital impressions from three intraoral scanners (Medit i900, 3Shape TRIOS 6, Dentsply Sirona Primescan 2) on a partially edentulous maxillary model using coded healing abutments at molar, incisor, and premolar sites. Transfer accuracy differed by site-specific abutment configuration, and scanner performance depended on the specific scanner, site, and component combination. The marginal scanner effect was not significant for translational or angular deviation.
why: Scanner accuracy for implant impressions with coded healing abutments may not be uniform across sites, so clinicians should not assume one scanner performs best in every situation until clinical validation is available.

headline: Single-cell atlas maps human periodontal ligament cells during orthodontic tooth movement
summary: Researchers built the first single-cell transcriptomic atlas of human periodontal ligament during orthodontic tooth movement, profiling pressure- and tension-side tissues at days 3 and 7 after force application. They analyzed 65,032 cells and found 15 populations, including a CTHRC1+ fibroblast subset enriched on the pressure side at day 3 that expressed TRPA1. In a mouse model, blocking TRPA1 or knocking it down reduced tooth movement, and C3 was identified as a possible downstream mediator of osteoclast-driven bone remodeling.
why: This basic-science work points to a possible molecular target, TRPA1 and C3 signaling, that could eventually influence how fast teeth move during orthodontic treatment, but it is preclinical and not yet a clinical guide.

headline: Postoperative oral irrigation helps stabilize mouth microbes after oral cancer reconstruction
summary: An exploratory randomized trial of 60 oral cancer patients who had free flap reconstruction compared postoperative rinsing with bipolar water against a hydrogen peroxide and sodium bicarbonate solution. Surgery reduced oral microbial diversity and shifted the community toward a more anaerobic, unstable state, while continued irrigation moved it toward a more stable structure. Wound infection rates and microbial composition did not differ between the two groups, but the bipolar water group reported better comfort, needed shorter irrigation times, and kept microbial diversity more stable.
why: For clinicians caring for patients after oral cancer reconstruction, bipolar water may be a comfortable alternative to peroxide-based irrigation, though the trial is exploratory and showed no difference in infection rates.

headline: Scoping review tracks gum inflammation markers during experimental gingivitis recovery
summary: A scoping review in the Journal of Periodontology examined immune and tissue-remodeling markers in gingival crevicular fluid as experimental gingivitis resolved. It covered 17 controlled trials from 1960 to 2024 involving 303 volunteers, and did not perform a meta-analysis because the studies were heterogeneous. The authors reported that IL-1β and ALP returned to baseline levels by the end of the resolution phase, which typically lasted 7 to 21 days.

headline: Mechanically crushed and hyaluronic acid-bound grafts shrink more in rabbit calvarial model
summary: In a preclinical study of ten rabbits with four vertical calvarial defects each, particulate porcine bone mineral alone (Control) and intact collagenated blocks kept their augmented volume at 8 weeks. Crushed collagenated blocks and particulate graft mixed with hyaluronic acid showed significant volumetric shrinkage, and mechanically manipulated grafts had shorter particles. New bone formation rose in all groups but was highest in the Control group.

headline: Periodontal management cost-effectiveness for CKD in Chinese adults depends on disease stage
summary: A Markov cohort model simulated Chinese adults aged 50 with periodontitis and chronic kidney disease, comparing usual care, scaling and root planing with maintenance, and comprehensive intensive management over 40 years. In early CKD, both periodontal strategies exceeded the willingness-to-pay threshold and were not cost-effective. In advanced CKD, both strategies were dominant, meaning they cost less and produced more QALYs than usual care, mainly because of avoided dialysis costs.
why: Suggests periodontal treatment may be economically justified for patients with advanced kidney disease, though the excerpt is a model-based study and the evidence linking periodontal care to kidney outcomes is observational.

headline: Epithelialized graft fragments vs. hemostatic sponge for palatal donor site healing
summary: A randomized clinical trial of 44 patients with deep lower incisor gingival recessions compared two ways to protect the palatal donor site after subepithelial connective tissue grafting: epithelialized fragments of the free gingival graft or a hemostatic sponge. Wound area was measured from standardized photographs over 28 days by a blinded examiner. The fragment group healed better than the sponge group at day 14 only, while pain scores and analgesic use were similar in both groups.

headline: Survey finds gaps in endodontic antibiotic knowledge among dental students
summary: An online survey of final-year undergraduate and postgraduate endodontic students across 10 dental schools in several countries assessed their knowledge of antibiotic use in endodontic care. Most respondents correctly identified when systemic antibiotics were not needed for localised infections and when they were indicated, such as acute apical abscess with systemic involvement or after replantation of an avulsed permanent tooth. Awareness of European (ESE) guidelines was much lower among undergraduates (49.1%) than postgraduates (82.6%), and prescribing knowledge varied by clinical scenario.
why: It suggests that dentists may see variation in antibiotic prescribing decisions tied to training, and that familiarity with current endodontic guidelines, especially ESE, cannot be assumed among newer graduates.

headline: Dentsply Sirona reports five years of sustainability progress, sets 2030 targets
summary: Dentsply Sirona marked five years since launching its "BEYOND" sustainability strategy, which rests on three pillars: Healthy Planet, Healthy Smiles and Healthy Business. The company says it has reported progress on its environmental, social and governance goals since 2021 and has set new sustainability targets for 2030.

headline: Orthodontists Say In-Office 3D Printing Hinges on Workflow, Staffing and Systems
summary: An article from Orthodontic Products reports that orthodontic practices succeeding with in-office 3D printing focus less on the printer and more on the workflow, staffing, and systems around it. It draws on three orthodontists who built in-office labs at different scales, who describe printing as one step in a longer sequence from scanning through washing, curing, and finishing. The piece notes that retainers are often the easiest starting point.
why: Dentists considering in-house production should plan the full workflow, staffing, and software processes before investing in equipment, since the hardware alone does not determine whether the lab pays off.

headline: Dr. Silverman's reflection: starting patient conversations with a mirror and a question
summary: This weekly column describes a hygienist who, noticing a patient's stated dissatisfaction with their smile on an updated dental history form, asks the patient to point out what they would like changed. The author argues that this open conversation, rather than a diagnosis or sales pitch, helps the patient feel heard and gives the team and doctor useful insight before treatment begins.

headline: Scotland confirms 3.75% NHS dental pay rise; BDA says practice funding is still short
summary: The Scottish government has confirmed a 3.75% pay increase for NHS general dental practitioners for the 2026/2027 financial year. The award matches the recommendation of the independent Review Body on Doctors' and Dentists' Remuneration, but the British Dental Association says it does not adequately address wider financial pressures on practices.

headline: Gargle Moves Dental Websites From WordPress to Custom Coded Builds
summary: Gargle, a dental marketing company, is changing how it builds websites for dental practices across North America, shifting away from WordPress templates toward a custom, fully coded infrastructure. The company says the change is aimed at better security, faster performance, and stronger SEO capabilities. Gargle president Jeff Richins said practices need a secure, high-performing digital foundation that turns online searches into new-patient opportunities.
