why: Dental practices relying on their website for new patient inquiries may see changes in how their sites are built, secured, and optimized if they work with Gargle.

headline: Factors linked to mid-buccal gingival recession severity in US adults, by periodontitis status
summary: A population study using NHANES 2011-2014 data from 5,891 dentate US adults aged 30 and older examined mid-buccal gingival recession and its associated factors. Recession was found in over 90% of adults at 1 mm or more, while severe recession (5 mm or more) was much less common. Age, sex, smoking, and education were associated with severity, with the pattern differing between adults with and without periodontitis.
why: Gingival recession is very common in this population, and age, male sex, and smoking (in people with periodontitis) appear to raise severity, which may help dentists target prevention and risk-based management.

headline: P. gingivalis PPAD gene expression tracks periodontitis more than rheumatoid arthritis status
summary: Researchers measured Porphyromonas gingivalis ppad gene expression in subgingival plaque across groups with preclinical, early, and established rheumatoid arthritis, with and without periodontitis. ppad expression was elevated in all periodontitis groups regardless of RA status, and its links to salivary CitH3 and serum ACPA appeared only in certain periodontitis subgroups. The authors concluded that PPAD is associated mainly with periodontitis and does not support a direct mechanistic link between PPAD and neutrophil extracellular traps in RA.
why: For dentists, this suggests periodontal bacterial activity is linked to periodontal inflammation more than to RA, so periodontitis remains a condition to manage on its own merits even in patients with early joint disease.

headline: HuFriedyGroup Signs Framework Deal to Acquire Mectron's Dental Business
summary: Hu-Friedy Mfg. Co., part of HuFriedyGroup, has signed a framework agreement to acquire the dental business of Mectron S.p.A., a maker of piezoelectric bone surgery and ultrasonic and air-polishing technologies. The deal follows a commercial partnership begun in 2023, when HuFriedyGroup started distributing Mectron's piezoelectric scaling and air-polishing devices in the United States and Canada. HuFriedyGroup says the acquisition would broaden its portfolio across prevention, implantology, and oral surgery and extend Mectron's technologies through its network in about 100 countries.

headline: Amalgam placement has dropped, but removal still carries wastewater duties
summary: U.S. amalgam placement has fallen sharply, yet many existing amalgam fillings remain in patients' mouths, and their removal is still regulated. Federal rules treat amalgam removal with the same wastewater obligations as placement. The article notes that the EPA identifies dental offices as the main source of mercury discharges to publicly owned treatment works.
why: Practices that have stopped placing amalgam may still be subject to wastewater compliance requirements whenever they remove old amalgam restorations, which are common in older patients.

headline: Sonic activation speeds bacterial reduction during root canal irrigation in lab study
summary: An in vitro study from researchers at an Indian dental institute compared 1% sodium hypochlorite alone with the same irrigant plus sonic activation using the SmartLite Pro EndoActivator. Activated irrigation reduced bacteria faster, reaching over 95% within one minute and over 99.9% within about two and a half minutes. The article, which is promotional in tone, also notes that more than 35% of canal surfaces are left untouched after instrumentation.
why: The findings suggest activating the irrigant may shorten disinfection time during root canal treatment, though the evidence is from an in vitro study and the source is a product-focused feed.

headline: Global CBCT study links missed canals and short fillings to post-treatment periapical lesions
summary: A multinational study pooled pre-existing CBCT scans from 54 countries to measure post-treatment periapical radiolucencies in root canal-treated teeth. About 69.5% of patients and 43.7% of treated teeth had at least one such radiolucency, with rates varying by region from 31.4% in Oceania to 62.3% in Africa. Missed canals, short fillings, and overfilling were associated with higher odds of these lesions, while unrestored or cavitated teeth showed a weaker association than crowned or overlaid teeth.
why: The findings reinforce that thorough canal location and proper working length filling are the treatment factors most tied to persistent periapical radiolucencies, which matters for endodontic quality and retreatment decisions.

headline: Irrigation Methods Affect Sealer Penetration and Dentin Erosion in Extracted Premolars
summary: An ex vivo study of 100 extracted human mandibular premolars compared ultrasonic activation, laser-activated irrigation, and the GentleWave system after minimally invasive or conventional instrumentation. Smear layer removal did not differ between the two instrumentation techniques for the same irrigation method. In minimally invasive canals, GentleWave and laser-activated irrigation produced greater apical sealer penetration than ultrasonic activation, and dentin erosion appeared in 12.5% of images, none of them from the GentleWave group.
why: Irrigation protocol may influence how well sealer reaches the apical canal and whether dentin is eroded, though the authors note the protocols differed in irrigant volume, exposure time, and sequence, so the results cannot be attributed to the activation technology alone.

headline: Larger apical enlargement linked to better strict healing in molar root canal treatment
summary: A systematic review with exploratory meta-analysis pooled five studies on apical enlargement and taper in primary root canal treatment of permanent mandibular molars. Two randomized trials found that +3 enlargement produced a higher strict periapical healing rate than +2 enlargement, while the effect of taper alone remained unclear. Single-arm data with final apical preparation sizes of #30 or smaller showed a descriptive pooled healing rate of about 72.9%.
why: For mandibular molars, preparing the apical canal slightly larger may improve periapical healing, though the evidence base is limited and taper's independent role is still uncertain.

headline: Machine learning models struggle to flag failed root canal healing in imbalanced data
summary: Researchers retrospectively trained logistic regression, random forest and SVM models on 276 single-tooth endodontic treatments to classify periapical healing as favorable or unfavorable after 12-18 months. Unfavorable healing occurred in 18.8% of cases, and a majority-class baseline reached 80.4% accuracy with zero sensitivity for failures. Imbalance handling improved detection of unfavorable outcomes, with an adjusted threshold reaching 90.9% sensitivity at the cost of many false positives; the authors say the findings are preliminary and need external validation.
why: Accuracy alone can hide failed endodontic cases, and these preliminary models are not ready for clinical use, though tooth type and baseline lesion size were the top predictors.

headline: Stakeholders say oral health is under-prioritised for dependent older adults
summary: Researchers ran semi-structured interviews with 36 stakeholders, including dependent older adults, carers, family members, health professionals and researchers, and analysed them thematically. Six themes emerged, covering experiences of oral health, current services, consequences of poor oral health, needed improvements, and outcomes that matter to patients. Participants agreed that oral health is not currently a priority for this group, and that care assistants are often reluctant to help with oral hygiene.
why: It suggests that oral health outcomes for dependent older patients are judged more by comfort, function and social ability than by clinical measures, which may shape how dentists approach care for these patients and their carers.

headline: Contralateral condyle shrinks after unilateral TMJ replacement, prosthesis stays put
summary: A retrospective study of 17 patients with an average age of 26 who had unilateral total temporomandibular joint replacement tracked 3D changes in the untreated condyle using CT scans taken right after surgery and at long-term follow-up (mean 13.2 months). The untreated side's condyle lost volume significantly, about 9.3% on average, with bone resorption on its posterior and superior surfaces. Simultaneous orthognathic surgery did not change this remodeling pattern, and the replacement condylar prosthesis moved less than 1 mm in each direction.
why: Surgeons planning TMJ replacement may need to account for bone changes on the opposite, non-operated joint, though the prosthesis itself appeared positionally stable in this small study.

headline: Synthetic self-retaining block yields more new bone than xenogeneic block in dog study
summary: In a split-mouth study in eight beagle dogs, staged alveolar ridge augmentation was compared using a self-retaining synthetic block versus a self-retaining xenogeneic block, each with particulate bone and a collagen membrane. Total augmented area did not differ between the two, but the synthetic side formed significantly more new bone (about 7.9 mm² versus 4.4 mm²). The synthetic side also showed greater horizontal distance to the most buccal new bone at mid-portion sites, reaching significance at one level after correction.

headline: In vitro study compares five impression methods for complete-arch implant accuracy
summary: Researchers tested five techniques for complete-arch implant impressions on a maxillary edentulous model with six implants: conventional open-tray splinted, direct intraoral scanning, calibrated intraoral scan protocol, extraoral photogrammetry, and intraoral photogrammetry. Each was repeated 10 times and compared against desktop scanning reference data for trueness and precision. Extraoral photogrammetry showed the best overall accuracy and precision, while calibrated intraoral scanning and conventional impressions had smaller deviations at distal implant sites under constrained alignment.
why: For complete-arch implant cases, the choice of impression method may affect fit accuracy, especially at distal implants, though these in vitro results have not been tested clinically.

headline: 3D-printed highly translucent zirconia crowns show fit and strength comparable to milled crowns
summary: Researchers compared 3D-printed and milled single crowns made from highly translucent 5Y zirconia, testing fit and fracture resistance under two debinding and presintering protocols. Printed crowns had larger cement gaps around the margin circumference but smaller occlusal gaps than milled crowns, and marginal gaps stayed under 80 µm in all groups. At 0.7 mm wall thickness printed crowns were stronger, while at 1.5 mm milled crowns were stronger, and the faster debinding protocol tended to give lower and more variable results for thicker printed crowns.
why: It suggests printed translucent zirconia crowns may be a viable alternative to milled ones, but a rapid debinding step may weaken thicker printed restorations, so protocol choice matters.

headline: Acidic aging roughens and softens two resin-ceramic crown materials, with differences by type
summary: Researchers compared a subtractively manufactured resin-ceramic (Vita Enamic) with an additively manufactured one (Permanent Crown) intended for definitive crowns. Disk specimens were polished and aged for 7 days in acidic artificial saliva at pH 5.0 to simulate an acidic oral environment, then tested for roughness, microhardness, and protein adsorption. Acidic aging increased surface roughness and reduced hardness for both materials, and the additively manufactured material adsorbed more protein than the subtractive one only after aging.

headline: Intraoral scans beat conventional impressions for short complete-arch implant spans only
summary: A systematic review of 23 studies (22 in vitro, 1 clinical) compared intraoral scanning techniques for complete-arch implants with the conventional splinted open tray impression. Plain intraoral scanning and scanning with scan aids were more accurate than conventional impressions for short implant spans, but less accurate for long spans. Evidence for the other scanning approaches was limited or insufficient.

headline: Direct pulp capping performs similarly to pulpotomy in carious primary molars
summary: A split-mouth randomized trial of 100 carious primary molars in children aged 4 to 9 compared direct pulp capping with pulpotomy, both using a calcium silicate-based putty (NeoPUTTY). Teeth were restored with glass ionomer and stainless-steel crowns and followed for 12 months. Success rates were 89.6% versus 91.7% at 6 months (p = 0.73) and were identical at 85.1% at 12 months, with preoperative factors not linked to outcome.
why: This short-term evidence suggests the less invasive direct pulp capping may achieve results comparable to pulpotomy for carious pulp exposures in primary molars, though the findings are limited to short-term follow-up.

headline: Ambulatory surgery centers outperform hospital outpatient departments for pediatric caries surgery
summary: A cross-sectional study of 2016 to 2020 Medicaid data from 28 states compared outcomes of pediatric dental caries surgeries done in ambulatory surgery centers with those done in hospital outpatient departments. Across eight racial and ethnic groups, surgeries in ambulatory surgery centers had shorter waits from the last dental visit, lower payments, and lower rates of emergency department visits and hospitalizations afterward. The benefits were seen across groups, with outcomes for most groups similar to those for White children.
why: For dentists referring children for surgical caries treatment, ambulatory surgery centers may offer faster access and lower costs than hospital outpatient departments, with no worse postoperative outcomes in this Medicaid population.

headline: Hospital peer consult line with dentistry used in 2,689 pediatric encounters
summary: A cross-sectional study reviewed electronic records from 2009 to 2023 for patients whose providers used Physician Direct Connect, a provider-to-provider consultation program with dentistry at a major children's hospital. Most requests came from physicians, mostly at urgent care sites, and dental trauma was the leading concern, with about 29% of consults ending in emergency department transfer.

headline: Scoping review maps collaborative care models linking medical and dental providers for children
summary: Researchers reviewed literature on multidisciplinary care in pediatric patients, using a five-stage scoping review method and three databases. Of 30 practice models, 14 were ranked high collaboration, 10 low, and 2 medium. High-collaboration models were linked to fewer missed appointments, more referrals, and higher dental use, while low-collaboration models were tied to reduced caries and restorative treatment and fewer preventive care gaps.
why: It suggests that coordinating with medical providers can help children keep dental appointments and receive preventive care, though barriers such as limited provider time, electronic health records, state practice laws, and interprofessional training must be addressed.

headline: School-based dental clinic compared with children's hospital dental clinic for pediatric caries care
summary: A retrospective study compared pediatric patients with caries treated over 17 months at a children's hospital dental clinic and a school-based dental clinic, using electronic health records and matching patients by age, sex, insurance status, and autism or ADHD diagnosis. The school-based clinic served a higher share of nonWhite patients, lower child opportunity index zip codes, and Medicaid or uninsured children, while the hospital clinic saw more Latino/Hispanic patients, non-English home languages, and children with autism. Among 556 matched pairs, school-based clinic patients had more visits, more completed treatment plans, more procedures completed, and better cooperation, with fewer general anesthesia referrals and without nitrous oxide available.
why: It suggests school-based clinics can deliver comprehensive pediatric treatment and reach underserved children, offering a model for practices or partnerships serving Medicaid and uninsured patients.

headline: Noise Levels and Speech Intelligibility in Pediatric Dental Treatment Settings
summary: Researchers measured sound with a sound level meter in four pediatric dental locations: an open bay, a quiet room, a moderate sedation suite, and an operating suite. They calculated articulation index values, a measure of speech intelligibility when background noise may obscure speech, and compared them with procedure type and chart data from 197 patients. The articulation index did not differ significantly by location or procedure, though values ranged from excellent to barely acceptable, and the authors concluded that noise affects speech intelligibility.
why: Clinicians working in open or shared pediatric spaces may find that background noise makes it harder for team members to communicate clearly, which bears on the workflow and safety of chairside communication.

headline: Use of the Hall technique rises at a US dental school over 12 years
summary: A retrospective review of a US dental school's records from 2012 through 2024 looked at how often the Hall technique was used for pediatric stainless steel crowns compared with conventional crowns. Of 25,837 crowns placed, 3,526 (13.6%) used the Hall technique, and that share grew significantly over the period. Pediatric dentistry residents placed the most Hall crowns, while predoctoral students increasingly adopted it over time.
why: The findings suggest the Hall technique is becoming a standard part of pediatric dental training and practice, which may prompt dentists to review how they place primary molar crowns.

headline: Photobiomodulation Lowers Stress and Pain in Children During Diagnostic Dental Visits
summary: A split-mouth randomized trial at the University of Maryland tested photobiomodulation (PBMT) with a multiwavelength LED device on 30 children aged 7 to 12 before cold pulp testing and gingival probing. PBMT produced smaller heart rate changes during cold testing and lower self-reported pain during gingival probing than the untreated control tooth, with no adverse events and preserved cold sensation.
why: This suggests PBMT could be a nonpharmacological option for calming young patients during routine diagnostic steps, though it is a single trial and its wider clinical role is not yet established.

headline: Buzzy and Vibradent vibrotactile devices ease pain and anxiety during pediatric anesthesia
summary: A study of 126 children aged 7 to 10 having dental extractions compared two vibrotactile devices, Buzzy and Vibradent, against a conventional syringe during local anesthesia. Both devices significantly reduced pain, anxiety, and salivary cortisol relative to the control group. Buzzy showed more favorable pain, heart rate, and anxiety scores and received the highest satisfaction ratings.
why: Both non-invasive vibrotactile tools may be practical options for making injections less distressing for young patients, with Buzzy appearing to perform somewhat better in this study.

headline: Pediatric dentists report high career satisfaction, with gaps across groups
summary: A cross-sectional survey of U.S. pediatric dentists, sent electronically to 6,322 members, drew 669 usable responses (11% response rate). Respondents were highly satisfied with patient care and professional relationships but less satisfied with income, stress, well-being, practice management, and the effects of COVID-19. Satisfaction varied significantly by gender, age, race, family status, practice ownership, work hours, patient volume, and Medicaid participation.
why: Practice owners and clinicians may find it useful that income, stress, and management are weak points, and that early-career dentists and those with heavy Medicaid caseloads show lower satisfaction, which points to where support could help retention.

headline: Cranberry juice studied for effects on plaque bacteria and acid production
summary: Two randomised controlled trials tested whether unsweetened cranberry juice can reduce bacterial growth and acid production in dental plaque from adults and children. The findings suggest the juice may influence plaque metabolism. The researchers say the results could guide further work on dietary approaches to caries prevention.
why: Although this is early research, it adds to evidence on how everyday beverages may affect plaque and caries risk, which could eventually shape dietary advice given to patients.

headline: Mectron to sell its dental business to Hu-Friedy
summary: Italian medical device maker Mectron has signed a framework agreement to sell its dental business to Hu-Friedy, part of US-based HuFriedyGroup. Mectron will keep manufacturing dental products for Hu-Friedy at its Carasco plant and will concentrate on medical applications. The transaction is expected to close by the end of 2026.
why: Hu-Friedy, a well-known instrument supplier, is taking over a dental product line, so practices may see changes in supplier relationships or product sourcing over the next year or so.

headline: Heating platelet-poor plasma extends PRF resorption for use as a barrier membrane
summary: The article describes how standard platelet-rich fibrin breaks down within about 2 to 3 weeks, which limits its use as a barrier. Recent studies reported that heating the platelet-poor plasma layer with Bio-Heat technology extends resorption to more than 4 months, creating extended PRF (e-PRF). The authors suggest e-PRF membranes could substitute for collagen membranes in guided bone regeneration.
why: If the extended PRF membranes perform as described, they could offer dentists a platelet-based alternative to collagen membranes for guided bone regeneration, though the excerpt is only an introduction and does not give clinical outcomes.

headline: DeW Life marks 10 years with November 2026 retreat in Charlotte
summary: Dental Entrepreneur Woman (DeW Life), founded by Anne Duffy, is holding its 10th anniversary retreat November 12–14, 2026, at The Ballantyne in Charlotte, North Carolina. More than 230 women from across the country are expected to attend a program of keynotes, DeW Talks, workshops, and networking focused on mentorship, leadership, and professional and personal growth. Registration has been extended through November 2, 2026.

headline: NIR-triggered Au@RCDs@GOx platform shows tumor suppression in oral cancer model
summary: Researchers built a near-infrared responsive nanoplatform, Au@RCDs@GOx, that combines photothermal ablation, glucose oxidase-generated hydrogen peroxide, enhanced chemodynamic therapy, and starvation therapy against oral squamous cell carcinoma. In a mouse xenograft model, intratumoral injection at an ultralow dose reportedly suppressed tumors by 95.7% with good biosafety. The platform also offers surface-enhanced Raman scattering signals that provide real-time feedback on oxidative stress in the tumor.

headline: New mouse toolkit targets ameloblast stages to study enamel formation
summary: Researchers built and verified a set of seven mouse genetic alleles, including stage-specific Cre recombinases and fluorescent reporters, for tracking ameloblasts, the cells that form enamel. The alleles were shown to work in adult mouse incisors and developing molars. The authors say the tools could help dissect enamel development and regeneration at much finer resolution than existing models.

headline: In vivo tube and tooth fragment models track vascular growth into the root canal space
summary: Researchers extended an earlier in vitro root canal tube model, in which dental pulp stem cell-derived endothelial-like cells formed vessel-like structures, into living mice. They also built a tooth fragment dorsal skinfold window chamber to watch host blood vessels grow into the canal space in real time. Host vessels grew in from surrounding tissue, but the engineered vessel-like structures did not develop into perfused, functional vessels within up to 50 days, and freshly prepared mineral trioxide aggregate was cytotoxic to implanted cells.
why: This is preclinical work using subcutaneous mouse models, so it does not change clinical practice yet, but it hints that freshly placed MTA may harm pulp-related cells and that engineered pulp vascularization remains unproven.

headline: Socioeconomic gaps in adolescent gum disease linked to oral health knowledge and brushing
summary: A study using data from China's Fourth National Oral Health Survey examined 7,113 adolescents across seven Sichuan regions. Teens from non-agricultural families, families with more educated parents, and fast-developing regions had lower odds of bleeding on probing, while adolescents in high-economic-level regions had higher odds of bleeding and calculus. Mediation analysis indicated that these socioeconomic differences were associated with gingivitis largely through oral health knowledge and brushing behavior.
why: Socioeconomic background appears to shape adolescent gingival health partly through hygiene knowledge and brushing, suggesting that education and behavior-focused prevention in disadvantaged groups may help reduce gum disease.

headline: Symptoms, not other clinical factors, linked to inflammation in root-filled teeth with apical periodontitis
summary: This cross-sectional study of 109 adult patients at a Copenhagen dental clinic biopsied periapical tissue from root-filled teeth with apical periodontitis and graded inflammation histologically. Inflammation differed significantly between asymptomatic and symptomatic cases, but demographic, dental history, clinical, and radiographic factors did not reflect inflammation level.
why: Whether a root-filled tooth with persistent radiolucency has symptoms may hint at how much inflammation is present, but other available clinical and radiographic findings were not reliable indicators, so clinicians should be cautious when relying on them for management decisions.

headline: CBCT segmentation and CARES classification guide treatment of dens invaginatus cases
summary: This case series describes three maxillary lateral incisors with dens invaginatus and periradicular disease, each assessed with CBCT and 3-dimensional segmentation of the tooth and root canal system. Cases were classified using both the Oehlers and the newer CARES systems. One case was treated with conventional CBCT-assisted access, while two anatomically complex cases required static guided endodontic access after conventional localization failed, and all showed healing at follow-up.
why: It suggests that 3D imaging and the CARES framework may help clinicians plan access and treatment for complex dens invaginatus anatomy, though the evidence comes from only three cases.

headline: ChatGPT-5.5 Poorly Matches Human Appraisal of Endodontic Systematic Reviews
summary: Researchers compared ChatGPT-5.5 with human experts in grading the methodological quality of 100 endodontic systematic reviews with meta-analysis, using the AMSTAR 2 tool. Overall confidence ratings agreed in about half the reviews under the primary criterion, and the AI rated far more reviews as critically low than the human consensus did. Item-level agreement varied widely across AMSTAR 2 domains, although the AI gave consistent answers across its three accounts.
why: Dentists relying on AI tools to quickly judge the quality of evidence reviews should not treat them as independent assessors, since human verification remains necessary.

headline: Orthodontic training urged to adopt patient-specific digital workflows
summary: A perspective in the Journal of Dental Education argues that postgraduate orthodontic curricula lag behind patient-specific data from CBCT and intraoral scanning, which is already collected at diagnosis, planning, and outcome assessment. Teaching in these areas still relies largely on population-normative references. The author weighs the benefits against risks such as overreliance on automated outputs and unequal access to digital tools, and proposes four curricular commitments: defining patient-specific digital competencies, progressive sequencing, assessment of reasoning, and accreditation requirements.
why: Dentists who supervise or hire orthodontic residents may see future graduates trained to use individualized 3D diagnosis and simulation, and accreditation changes could eventually shape what new specialists bring to practice.

headline: Survey finds about one-third of North American orthodontic residencies use teleorthodontics
summary: A cross-sectional survey sent to accredited postgraduate orthodontic residency programs in North America got 41 completed responses, a 60.3% response rate. Of those, 13 programs (31.7%) reported teaching teleorthodontics, and 12 (29.3%) reported using it in clinical practice, with most of the clinical users also using AI-driven features. Programs that had adopted it viewed it positively, but lack of institutional priority, privacy and data security concerns, and limited curriculum time were the main barriers for those that had not.
why: It suggests teleorthodontics is spreading slowly at the institutional level, so practicing dentists and specialists may see its use grow gradually, with data privacy remaining a key concern.

headline: Case report urges minimally invasive approach to anterior aesthetic rehabilitation
summary: An opinion-style case article argues that social media has pushed dentists toward fast, dramatic smile results at the expense of patience and precision. It describes a 28-year-old patient with a reverse smile line, showing limited display of upper front teeth and excess lower tooth display. The author notes two treatment philosophies were weighed, the first being a more aggressive approach that would open the vertical dimension and add length to the upper anterior teeth.
why: It is a reminder to consider orthodontic repositioning and underlying airway or breathing concerns before choosing extensive tooth preparation for an aesthetic complaint.

headline: Dentist Argues Intraoral Scanning and AI Are Becoming Core to Practice Performance
summary: A cosmetic dentist and race car driver, Dr. Todd Snyder, writes that intraoral scanners are shifting from optional upgrades to foundational technology. He compares a high-performing dental practice to a race car, where integrated systems and data drive success. The excerpt also promotes a free CE webinar by the same author on October 28 that follows up on the article.
why: It suggests dentists may need to view digital scanning as central to diagnosis, treatment planning, lab work, and practice profitability rather than as an optional add-on.

headline: Podcast explores the origins of dental fear and how it may be treated
summary: An episode of the Dentistry Unmasked podcast features hosts Drs. Pam Maragliano and Brian Nový speaking with Dr. Kelly Daly, a clinical psychologist and researcher at NYU. The discussion covers where dental fear comes from and the science behind treating it.
why: Dentists dealing with anxious patients may find the conversation useful for understanding fear's roots and approaches to easing it, though the excerpt itself does not describe specific treatment results.

headline: In vitro study compares water solubility of three tricalcium silicate root canal sealers
summary: Researchers immersed standardized specimens of BioRoot RCS, Bio-C Sealer, and NeoSealer Flo in distilled water under ISO 6876:2012 guidance and measured mass loss over 1440 hours. Bio-C Sealer was the most soluble at 11.56%, while BioRoot RCS (5.81%) and NeoSealer Flo (4.97%) were less soluble, though all three exceeded the 3% ISO limit. BioRoot RCS and NeoSealer Flo did not differ significantly from each other but both resisted dissolution better than Bio-C Sealer.
why: Solubility may affect how long a bioceramic sealer maintains its seal, so sealer choice may matter in cases where long-term stability is important, though the authors note that more long-term research is needed.

headline: Nanofibrous scaffold and laser photobiomodulation used for an incisor with root resorption
summary: A case report describes managing internal root resorption and an open apex in a maxillary central incisor of a 25-year-old man with prior dental trauma. The approach combined revascularization, a nanofibrous scaffold at the apical third, an MTA plug, laser-assisted disinfection, adjunctive photobiomodulation, and a bioceramic sealer, followed by a zirconia crown. At 24 months, a periapical radiograph showed apical closure, resolution of the periapical lesion, and preserved tooth function.

headline: Methotrexate mix-up causes severe oral ulcers and blood toxicity in a 68-year-old woman
summary: A case report describes a 68-year-old woman with inflammatory arthritis who developed acute methotrexate toxicity after taking methotrexate instead of mirtazapine for about a month, due to a pharmacy dispensing error. She presented with oral erosions resembling erythema multiforme and blistering skin lesions, and blood tests showed reduced leukocytes and erythrocytes. After methotrexate was stopped and she received supportive treatment, the lesions resolved and her counts improved before discharge.
why: Oral erosions resembling erythema multiforme should prompt dentists to ask about recent medication use and possible dispensing errors, especially with high-risk drugs like methotrexate.

headline: Coronectomy as an alternative to extraction for high-risk mandibular third molar
summary: A case report describes a 55-year-old woman with pain and food trapping near a left mandibular third molar that lay close to the mandibular canal. Clinicians chose coronectomy, removing the crown and leaving the roots at least 3 mm below the alveolar crest to protect the inferior alveolar nerve. At two years, clinical and radiographic review showed good healing and bone repair with no root migration.
why: It offers a conservative option for impacted third molars near the nerve when extraction carries a high risk of paresthesia, though it applies only to carefully selected cases and needs periodic follow-up of the retained roots.

headline: Photoinitiator choice alters mechanical properties of experimental resin cements
summary: Researchers compared three experimental light-curable resin cements, each using a different photoinitiator system, against a commercial resin cement (RelyX Veneer). They measured flexural strength, flexural modulus, and Knoop surface microhardness. The photoinitiator type significantly changed mechanical properties, and the BAPO-containing cements performed comparably to or better than the commercial control.
why: Suggests that the photoinitiator chemistry in resin cements can affect how strong and hard the set material is, which may matter when choosing cements for restorations, though this is a laboratory study.

headline: Tongue pain as first sign of glossopharyngeal neuralgia in a 73-year-old woman
summary: This case report describes a 73-year-old woman with left-sided pain in the back of the tongue, later diagnosed as classical glossopharyngeal neuralgia, a rare orofacial pain disorder. The diagnosis was made using clinical findings along with high-resolution MRI and angiography. The authors note that the condition is easily confused with other cranial nerve neuralgias and with non-neuropathic problems such as oropharyngeal infections and reflux.
why: Unexplained tongue pain can stem from a neurologic cause, so dentists should consider glossopharyngeal neuralgia in the differential and refer patients promptly when a dental cause is not found.

headline: Single-shade composites match conventional resins in staining resistance
summary: Researchers compared color, translucency, and coffee-staining susceptibility of two single-shade composite resins with two conventional composites using 48 disc specimens. After seven days in coffee, all composites darkened in lightness and shifted toward red and yellow, but the overall color change did not differ significantly between the single-shade and conventional materials. The single-shade resins showed greater translucency and, for one product, higher lightness.

headline: Case report describes an unusually pink lipoma on the ventral tongue
summary: This case report describes an atypical oral lipoma, a fairly uncommon soft tissue lesion made mostly of mature fat cells. Oral lipomas can have several histologic variants containing tissues such as spindle cells, cartilage, or salivary glands, and they usually appear on the buccal mucosa with a yellow to yellow-pink color. The authors report a moderately pink lipoma located on the ventral tongue, which is an unusual presentation.
why: Dentists may encounter oral lipomas with atypical coloring or locations, so this case is a reminder to consider them in the differential diagnosis of tongue lesions.

headline: High-power diode laser manages recurrent proliferative verrucous leukoplakia in one case
summary: A case report describes treating proliferative verrucous leukoplakia, a persistent and recurrent oral potentially malignant disorder, in a 54-year-old male smoker with extensive white plaques across the mouth. The patient underwent nine surgical sessions with a 980-nm diode laser at 1.5 W in continuous mode, spaced 45 to 60 days apart. At 18 months after the first treatment, he reported satisfaction, showed no significant recurrence, and had reduced his tobacco use.
why: It offers a single case suggesting high-power laser surgery may be an option for controlling extensive PVL lesions that are hard to treat, though one case cannot establish general effectiveness and close long-term monitoring remains essential.

headline: Case report: managing invasive cervical resorption in a maxillary canine
summary: A case report describes treating a patient with class 3Ap invasive cervical resorption (ICR) in the maxillary left canine, an aggressive form of external root resorption with unclear, likely multifactorial causes. Cone beam CT guided diagnosis and planning, and treatment combined endodontic therapy, surgery, and restoration with a bioactive resin containing a surface-treated prereacted glass ionomer filler. At 6-month follow-up, the tooth showed clinical and radiographic success with no recurrence.
why: It illustrates that early diagnosis with CBCT and interdisciplinary endodontic and surgical management may preserve teeth affected by ICR and avoid extraction.

headline: Unsweetened Cranberry Juice Linked to Slower Plaque Growth in Small Study
summary: A University of Illinois Chicago study compared unsweetened 100% cranberry juice with a sweetened cranberry cocktail containing 27% pure juice, in 14 children and eight adults who skipped brushing beforehand. Plaque exposed to the pure juice grew more slowly, and participants who drank it showed lower acid production than those who drank the sweetened beverage.

headline: One-shade vs multi-shade flowable composites for cervical lesions: 18-month trial
summary: A double-blind, split-mouth randomized trial compared a one-shade flowable composite with a multi-shade flowable composite for restoring non-carious cervical lesions in 62 participants. Objective color differences did not differ significantly between the two materials, and 18-month retention was 98.4% for the one-shade and 100% for the multi-shade product. Visual color match scored higher for the multi-shade material at 18 months, though all restorations evaluated for color remained clinically acceptable.
why: A one-shade flowable may simplify cervical lesion restorations by removing shade selection while keeping acceptable color match and performance, though the multi-shade material scored better visually at 18 months.

headline: Review examines stem cells from baby teeth and their cell-free derivatives in regenerative medicine
summary: This literature review looks at stem cells from human exfoliated deciduous teeth (SHED) as a basis for cell-free regenerative approaches. It covers secretomes, extracellular vesicles, extracellular matrix, conditioned medium, and decellularized matrices, drawing mainly on preclinical studies from PubMed and Web of Science. The authors report that these products may support tissue repair through bioactive molecules and effects on the host environment, but standardized preparation, mechanistic validation, and safety and efficacy testing are still needed.
why: Cell-free SHED-derived products could eventually offer a ready-to-use option for regenerative dentistry that avoids some risks of transplanting living cells, but the evidence is still preclinical and not ready for patient use.

headline: Intraoral scanning shows feasibility for 3D soft-tissue volume assessment in mucogingival surgery
summary: This proof-of-concept study tested a digital workflow using intraoperative scans on five patients with gingival recessions treated at 14 sites, with eight sites receiving a subepithelial connective tissue graft and six treated without grafting. Scans taken at several stages were compared to reconstruct external and internal soft-tissue volumes and initial graft volume. External volume was numerically higher at 1 month and lower at 3 months, but pairwise differences were not significant, and the authors call for validation in larger, standardized samples.
why: It suggests intraoral scanning may eventually supplement conventional clinical measurements for tracking soft-tissue changes after gum grafting and recession surgery, though the evidence is preliminary and based on a very small sample.

headline: AAO Forms Sleep-Disordered Breathing Task Force to Review Clinical Guidance
summary: The American Association of Orthodontists has created a seven-member task force to examine new research and challenges to its current stance on sleep-disordered breathing. The group includes orthodontic and medical experts who will work with other organizations and recommend whether AAO policies and clinical resources should change. The excerpt also notes that the AAO recently issued a position paper on artificial intelligence that emphasizes the orthodontist as the final decision-maker.
why: Orthodontists may see AAO guidance on sleep-disordered breathing change over time, and the AI framework reinforces that the clinician keeps final responsibility for patient care.

headline: Micro-screws for mandibular occlusal plane control in edge-to-edge bites
summary: The article covers adult patients with a Class II skeletal pattern and bimaxillary dentoalveolar protrusion, who may have reduced overjet or an edge-to-edge incisal relationship. It argues that treatment planning should address sagittal and vertical control, including occlusal plane orientation, and notes that dentoalveolar compensation may already be near its limit, restricting incisor retraction and overbite correction through tooth movement alone.
why: For these cases, tooth movement alone, and aligners in particular, may not achieve enough incisor retraction or overbite correction, so clinicians may need to plan occlusal plane management as part of the biomechanics.
